The southward migration occurs by individuals born in the northern regions going all the way to the high-elevation forests of a southern country. They've tagged butterflies all throughout a specific region and found them again in that southern country.
These butterflies do not migrate to the southern continent. They migrate to a northern country.

These butterflies are not on a 2-generation per trip. The individuals overwintering in a specific location move to the southern US where they breed and then perish. Their offspring migrate to the northern regions whereupon they have their 2nd, 3rd, and often 4th generations. These 3rd and 4th generation individuals (the non-breeders) depart from the north and migrate all of the way to the overwintering location. Some small number may peel off and resume breeding in the south, but there is no evidence that they then go southward. Some of the 5th generation individuals may stay in the south or they may venture to the overwintering location (this part is not well understood). Nevertheless, most individuals at the end of summer move a couple thousand miles when migrating.

The change in seasons opens the US and Canada to breeding. An adult monarch butterfly moving into the southern US will lay her complement of eggs (several hundred) and then die. Her offspring continue the march northward because milkweed in the south senesces under the hot temperatures and is no longer available. The migration evolved to take advantage of the seasonal availability of resources that wouldn't otherwise be available if they had stayed put.
